archetype.name: Retooling (leaky structure)
archetype.definition: A team two seasons removed from a 116-point first-place finish that still has front-line scorers but now gives up more shots than anyone, and no longer has the goaltending to cover for it.

report.headline: Three straight wins mask the league's most porous defense; the slide is structural.
report.take:
Winnipeg is 7-8-3, sixth of eight in the Central and 27th of 32 on the site. The drop from the top is steep. In 2024-25 this franchise had 116 points, a first-place site rank and the league's best defense, with goalies at 40.9 GSAx. Last season it fell to 82 points and a 7.6 GSAx. This season it is at -2.7. The team that won by keeping the puck out of its net has lost that identity, and the current pace of 77 standings points would be a further step down.

The core problem is volume against. Winnipeg allows 33.2 shots a game, last in the league and 6.2 above the league average, and its 5-on-5 shares (47.9% xGF, 48% CF) say it is being out-chanced, not just outshot from the perimeter. Teams that bleed shots like that need a goalie stealing games, and neither Stuart Skinner (.883) nor Nico Daws (.886) is doing it. The penalty kill at 71.7% sits 25th. The offense is not the disaster the 26th-ranked goals-per-game suggests: Winnipeg puts 28.7 shots a game on net, ninth in the league, and Kyle Connor has 13 goals on 74 shots.

What the numbers hide runs both ways. The all-situations PDO of 97.6 is 30th, and the team's 9.5% shooting is well under the league's 11.6%. Gabriel Vilardi and Dawson Mercer have one goal each on 34 shots apiece, and that should correct. Against that, the 5-on-5 PDO is a near-average 99.3, so even strength is not unusually cursed. The Pts vs Goal Diff of +1.5 (eighth) means the record is, if anything, slightly kind to a -14 goal differential. The recent three-game win streak followed a nine-game losing streak, and the last five games still ran at -0.8 a game, essentially the season rate.

Where it heads: some scoring will come back as the shooting normalizes. But a team giving up shots at this rate, with a below-average kill and no goaltending edge, profiles as a lottery-adjacent club rather than a bubble team. Until the shot count against comes down, a streak like this one is noise on top of a negative goal differential.

strengths.title: Connor and the top six produce
strengths.body: Kyle Connor has 13 goals and 19 points, sixth on the left-wing tab. Mark Scheifele (18 points) and Cole Perfetti (14, 15th among centers) give the top of the lineup genuine punch, and all three sit above 52% xGF. This is talent-driven and should hold. It is the main reason Winnipeg can outscore weaker teams.

strengths.title: Shot volume with finishing upside
strengths.body: Winnipeg generates 28.7 shots a game, ninth in the league, yet converts at only 9.5% against a league mark of 11.6%. Depth forwards like Vilardi and Mercer are snakebitten on decent volume. Expect goals per game to drift up from its 26th-place rank as that shooting rate normalizes.

strengths.title: Pionk anchors a B- blueline
strengths.body: The defense grades B-, the best group on the roster. Neal Pionk carries 24.26 minutes a night and ranks 14th on the defense tab. Dylan Samberg's 56.4% xGF is the best on-ice share among regulars. The problem is less the top pair than the shot volume the whole team concedes.

concerns.title: Worst shot suppression in the league
concerns.body: At 33.2 shots allowed a game, Winnipeg is 32nd of 32 and 6.2 shots above the league average. The below-50% xGF share shows the chances are real, not just volume from distance. The bottom of the lineup is part of it: Morgan Barron (40.4%) and Adam Lowry (43.9%) are being caved in. This is the structural flaw, and nothing in the recent games suggests it is fixed.

concerns.title: No goaltending bailout, weak kill
concerns.body: The 2024-25 team had goalies 40.9 goals above expected. This season's pair is at -2.7, with Daws at -2.2 in his five starts, and the combined .881 save % ranks 26th. Add a 71.7% penalty kill and the margin for error disappears. Skinner's near-zero GSAx says he is roughly average on bad shot quality, so do not count on a big rebound here.

concerns.title: The win streak isn't a turnaround
concerns.body: The three straight wins came after a nine-game skid, and the last five games still ran at a -0.8 goal differential a game, matching the season. Two of those wins were one-goal games, one in overtime. With Pts vs Goal Diff already at +1.5, the standings are not hiding a better team.

trend.note: A four-win October included a nine-game losing streak; November opened 3-1 with three straight wins. The goal differential per game hasn't moved, so the swings are in results, not in the level of play.

weekAhead.headline: Two top-eight opponents before a soft landing in Chicago
weekAhead.body:
The week opens against two of the league's better teams. New Jersey (13-5-0, seventh on the site) owns the second-best xGF share at 57.3% and allows a league-low 19.9 shots a game, the exact opposite profile of Winnipeg. Then comes a trip to Dallas (10-5-2, eighth), which pairs the league's best penalty kill at 89.7% with goaltending worth 8.3 goals above expected. A Winnipeg team that relies on volume shooting will find little of it in either game.

Chicago closes the week, and it is the softest opponent on the schedule: 4-13-1, 31st on the site, last in goal differential and 32nd in all-situations PDO. Realistically Winnipeg needs special teams against New Jersey to steal points, then has to take care of business against the Blackhawks. Two of three would be a good week; one is the likelier result.

keyMatchups.title: Winnipeg's power play vs. Devils' kill
keyMatchups.body: New Jersey's penalty kill is 29th at 67.6%, and its goaltending grades C- with -5.8 GSAx. That is the one soft spot in an otherwise dominant team. Winnipeg's power play converts at 21.8%, so drawing penalties is its clearest path to goals in a game it will likely lose on shots. The Devils also give an above-league share of their points against to defensemen, which suits Pionk.

keyMatchups.title: Dallas shuts the doors
keyMatchups.body: Dallas is third in goals against per game, kills 89.7% of penalties and has holds opposing forwards furthest under their usual output of all but two teams. Its own offense ranks 25th, so this projects as a low-event game where Winnipeg's shot volume edge must translate. Expect Winnipeg to need a strong night from its goalie to stay close.

keyMatchups.title: Connor against Chicago's wingers defense
keyMatchups.body: Chicago allows 4.56 points a game to wingers, more than a point over what those players usually produce, the 31st-ranked mark in the league. Its goaltending grades D-. This is the game for Connor and the top six to cash in, and for Winnipeg's low shooting percentage to start correcting.

weekAhead.watch: Shots against in the New Jersey game: if a team that allows a league-low 19.9 shots a game still outshoots Winnipeg badly, nothing has changed structurally.

restOfSeason.body:
The 77-point pace is the honest baseline, with modest upside. Shooting at 9.5% will likely climb toward league norms as Vilardi, Mercer and the depth forwards start converting, which should lift the offense out of the bottom seven. But the defensive profile is the bigger issue: the most shots allowed in the league, a sub-50% expected-goals share, a 25th-ranked kill and goaltending near zero GSAx. That isn't bad luck that fades; it's how the team plays right now.

The positive Pts vs Goal Diff suggests close-game results may give a little back. Barring a real goaltending turn or a sharp drop in shots allowed, I expect Winnipeg to finish in the 74-84 point range, outside the playoff picture. That would be a second straight season well below the 110-plus point standard of 2023-24 and 2024-25.
swingFactors: Whether shots against come down from the league's worst

confidence.note: 18 games is small, but shot rates and xGF stabilize early and line up with last season's decline.
